title: SNIP, a Statistics-Sensitive Background Treatment for the Quantitative Analysis of PIXE Spectra in Geoscience Applications
venue: Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research B34

citations.claim: Ryan et al. proposed the Statistics-sensitive Non-linear Iterative Peak-clipping (SNIP) algorithm, which estimates the background of a spectrum by iteratively replacing each channel value with the lesser of itself or the mean of two symmetrically placed neighbors.

The SNIP algorithm compresses the dynamic range of channel counts using a double log transformation G(y) = log(log(y + 1) + 1) prior to peak clipping, which reduces the required number of iterations from approximately 700 to approximately 24.

SNIP employs a low-statistics digital filter that adaptively smooths low-count regions of a spectrum while preserving peak shapes and inter-peak valleys, avoiding the trade-off inherent in fixed-width n-point smoothing.

Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated that the SNIP background algorithm maintains stable trace element concentrations over a 100-fold change in counting statistics, with an average high-to-low statistics ratio of 0.98 and standard deviation of 0.09.

Simpler peak-clipping and family-of-parabolas background algorithms systematically overestimate peak areas as counting statistics decrease, with errors up to a factor of 4 for trace elements near the detection limit.
The SNIP algorithm is parameter-free and independent of detector energy calibration, enabling batch processing of spectra without user-adjustable settings.

SNIP is an early and influential iterative baseline estimation method for spectral data, originally developed for PIXE X-ray spectra but subsequently adopted in other spectroscopy and signal processing domains.

do_not_claim: SNIP was designed for or applied to chromatographic baseline correction
SNIP uses optimization or regularization to estimate the baseline
SNIP is a learning-based or data-driven method
SNIP produces a smooth baseline in the same sense as penalized least-squares methods
